content.text: 升级harness版本
升级harness版本

tools.name: ask_user_question
tools.description: Ask the user a concise question when you need confirmation, a choice, or missing information before proceeding. Send one or more questions, each with a stable id that will be echoed in the answer.

questions.description: Questions to ask the user before continuing.

id.description: Stable id for this question; echoed in the answer.

question.description: The specific question to ask the user.

header.description: Optional short heading for the question, such as "Confirm" or "Choose Mode".

options.description: Optional choices to show the user. If you recommend one, put it first and append "(Recommended)" to that label.

description.description: One sentence explaining the tradeoff or impact.

multi_select.description: Whether the user may select more than one option. Defaults to false.

tools.name: create_goal
tools.description: Create one persisted same-session completion goal when the current direct human request is a long-running objective that should continue across autonomous goal rounds. You may infer that intent without requiring the user to say "create a goal". Do not use this for trivial single-turn work. Execution rejects non-human and subagent authority.

objective.description: The concrete completion objective inferred from the direct human request.

max_goal_rounds.description: Optional positive safe-integer limit on automatic continuation rounds.

tools.name: edit
tools.description: Edit an existing UTF-8 text file by replacing literal text.

file_path.description: Path to edit, resolved by the filesystem backend.

old_string.description: Literal text to replace. Must match exactly.

new_string.description: Literal replacement text. Use an empty string to delete the match.

replace_all.description: Replace all matches. Defaults to false; when false, old_string must appear exactly once.

sandbox_permissions.description: The wider sandbox mode this file operation needs. Only valid as a one-shot retry of an operation the sandbox just denied; requires justification and user approval.

justification.description: Required with sandbox_permissions: one sentence for the user explaining why this exact file operation needs the wider access.

tools.name: exit_plan_mode
tools.description: Use only in plan mode. Present your plan for the user's review and, on approval, leave plan mode. Send the COMPLETE plan as markdown, starting with a # heading that names it. The user may approve (carry out the plan from your next step) or keep planning — their feedback comes back in the tool result; revise and present again.

plan.description: The complete plan, as markdown, starting with a # heading that names it.

tools.name: get_goal
tools.description: Read the current same-session goal, including its exact id/revision, objective, phase, completed continuation rounds, round limit, blocker reason when present, and whether another continuation is armed. Call this before updating a goal.

tools.name: glob
tools.description: Find files whose paths match a glob pattern. Returns matching file paths — never directories — including hidden and ignored files (VCS metadata directories are excluded). Up to 100 paths come back in modification-time order; a larger result returns the first 100 paths in modification-time order, says so, and reports where the complete sorted list was saved. This tool does not enumerate directory entries.

pattern.description: Glob pattern to match file paths against (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.js"). A pattern with no "/" matches the basename at any depth, so "*" and "*.ts" both search the whole tree; include a separator to anchor the depth.

path.description: Directory to search in. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

tools.name: grep
tools.description: Search file contents with a ripgrep regular expression. Returns matching lines with line numbers, grouped by file. Returns the first 250 matches inline; a capped result reports where the complete match list was saved. Use read on a matched file for surrounding context.

pattern.description: Regular expression to search for (ripgrep syntax).

path.description: File or directory to search. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

include.description: One glob filter for which files to search (e.g. "*.ts", "*.{js,jsx}"). Not a list; negation is not supported.

tools.name: interrupt_agent
tools.description: Request cancellation of a background agent's current turn by its agent id. The target may be your direct child or a deeper agent created under you. Only the current turn stops: messages already queued for the agent stay parked until a later send_message, agents it started keep running, and the agent itself stays available for follow-ups. This call returns as soon as the stop request is accepted, so the target may keep running briefly; interrupting an agent that already finished is an accepted no-op.

agent_id.description: The agent id of the running agent to interrupt.

tools.name: job_kill
tools.description: Request cancellation of a running background job by job id. Returns immediately; the job settles as killed once its work actually stops.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

reason.description: Optional short reason, recorded in the log and forwarded to the job.

tools.name: job_list
tools.description: List your background jobs (running and finished) with their ids, kinds, and statuses.

tools.name: job_output
tools.description: Read a background job. Stream jobs return only output since the previous read; final-output jobs return their result after settlement. Every response ends with `[status: ...]`. Reads are non-blocking unless `wait: true`, which waits up to the configured cap.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

wait.description: Block until the job reaches a terminal status or the timeout expires. A timed-out wait returns [status: running] and leaves the job alive.

timeout_ms.description: Max wait in milliseconds (only meaningful with wait: true). Defaults to the configured wait timeout; capped by the configured maximum.

tools.name: list_agents
tools.description: List your continuable background subagents by durable id and label. Use it to recall which ones you started, not to poll for completion — you are told when one finishes. Status comes from the live registry: running means the agent is working right now, idle means it is loaded but between turns (it may be waiting on agents it started), and ready means it exists only in storage — resumable, not terminal, and not a result waiting to be collected; a `send_message` steers a running child at its nearest step boundary or starts a turn for an idle or ready child, and a direct child remains a `send_message` candidate in every status. The snapshot is not a delivery promise — `send_message` performs the authoritative check and may still fail. Children that could not be read are reported as diagnostics instead of being silently dropped. Scope `descendants` walks the whole tree below you in stable pre-order, annotating each entry with its durable direct-parent session id and depth. You may use `send_message` only for depth-1 entries; deeper entries are candidates for `interrupt_agent` only.

scope.description: children (default) lists direct children only; descendants walks the complete tree below you.

tools.name: present
tools.description: Declare existing files accessible through the Session filesystem as final deliverables. When a file you create or update is an output the user asked to receive, you must call present after writing it and before your final response, including files created through Bash or code execution. Mentioning its path in your reply does not replace this call. The files must already exist. The user opens the current source files; their contents are not copied or preserved.

path.description: Path of an existing regular file. Relative paths use the Session working directory.

description.description: Brief description for the user.

tools.name: pwsh
tools.description: Execute a PowerShell command (`pwsh -Command`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh pwsh process: no state (cwd, variables, functions) persists between calls — pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Paths use native Windows form (`C:\...`); read environment variables with `$env:NAME`. Non-zero exits are reported as `[exit code: N]`. Current harness environment facts are exposed through managed `$env:DSH_*` variables; inspect them when needed. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` — a policy denial, not a bug in the command; do not retry another way. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. On Windows a force-killed command settles as `[exit code: 1]` without a signal marker — treat it as an interruption, not a command failure. Set `run_in_background: true` for long-running commands: the call returns a job id immediately; read its output with `job_output` and stop it with `job_kill`. Under the Windows sandbox, read-only pwsh runs in PowerShell ConstrainedLanguage mode, while workspace-write stays in FullLanguage unless host policy says otherwise. In read-only, prefer cmdlets and core types (`[string]`, `[datetime]`, `[regex]`, `[guid]`); .NET static calls (`[System.IO.*]::`, `[math]::`), `Add-Type`, COM objects, and reflection fail with "only core types" errors. `-f` formatting, property access, and core cmdlets work. In both confined modes, programs cannot open named pipes, so a command that captures another program's output through piped stdio (Node.js `child_process.spawn`/`exec` with the default `stdio: 'pipe'`) fails with EPERM, while `stdio: 'inherit'` and `stdio: 'ignore'` spawns work and PowerShell's own pipelines are unaffected. That EPERM is the documented boundary: do not retry the command another way — escalate the exact command once or restructure it to avoid capturing output. Attempting a command the sandbox may deny is safe and expected: run it and read the marker rather than assuming the denial. When a command is denied and a wider mode would let it succeed, escalate immediately in the same turn — the one sanctioned exception to a denial: retry the exact same command once with `sandbox_permissions` (the narrowest wider mode that suffices) plus a one-sentence `justification`. Do not detour through chat to ask permission first — the approval prompt raised by that retry is how the user consents. If the session states approval prompts are disabled, there is no exception: a denial is final — do not set `sandbox_permissions`. Never escalate speculatively: ground the request in a real denial — normally the one this command just hit; escalating up front is fine only when this session already denied the same access. A rejected escalation is final for that command — stop and explain, never work around it — but it does not forbid attempting or escalating other commands later.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "Get-Process" → "List running processes".

timeoutMs.description: Timeout in milliseconds. The executor applies its configured default and cap, and kills the command on expiry.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

sandbox_permissions.description: The wider sandbox mode this command needs. Only valid as a one-shot retry of a command the sandbox just denied; requires justification and user approval.

justification.description: Required with sandbox_permissions: one sentence for the user explaining why this exact command needs the wider access.

tools.name: ralph
tools.description: Run a foreground fresh-agent Ralph loop toward one immutable objective. Use only when the direct human explicitly asks for Ralph or fresh-agent iteration. Each round opens a new child with no parent conversation or prior child session; the shared workspace is long-term memory, and only a bounded structured report crosses rounds. The call returns when a worker reports completion or a concrete blocker, or at the round limit. Ordinary long-running same-session work belongs to goal tools.

objective.description: The immutable completion objective for every fresh Ralph round.

maxRounds.description: Optional positive safe-integer round cap, bounded by the deployment ceiling.

tools.name: read
tools.description: Read a UTF-8 text file and return line-numbered content.

file_path.description: Path to read, resolved by the filesystem backend.

offset.description: 1-based first line to return. Defaults to 1.

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to return. Defaults to 2000.

tools.name: read_image
tools.description: Read a PNG/JPEG/WebP/GIF file and return the image itself. A path without a file extension is accepted; the format is detected from the file content, so normalized attachment paths can be passed directly without copying or renaming. Harness validates and downscales large supported images before the next model request, so use this tool directly instead of installing image libraries or creating thumbnails merely to inspect an image. Independent files may be read concurrently in small batches. Requires the current model to accept image input.

file_path.description: Path to the image file, resolved by the filesystem backend.

tools.name: send_message
tools.description: Send a message to a direct continuable child by its agent id. If you are a resident continuable child, you may also target your direct parent. If the target is still working, the message steers its nearest step; if it is idle, the message starts a turn. This call returns no answer from the agent — only confirmation that the message was delivered. A failure means the message was NOT delivered.

agent_id.description: The agent id of your direct continuable child, or your direct parent when you are a resident continuable child.

message.description: The message to deliver to the agent.

tools.name: skill
tools.description: Load the full instructions for an available skill. Call this with the exact skill name from the session skill catalog before acting on a task that names or clearly matches that skill.

name.description: The exact skill name from the available skills list.

tools.name: subagent
tools.description: Delegate a self-contained task to a subagent (a separate agent that works in its own context) to offload focused, independent work — research, a scoped implementation, an analysis — so it does not consume this conversation's context. The subagent returns its result, not its intermediate steps. Give it a complete, standalone prompt: it does not see this conversation. This tool runs in the background by default, immediately returns a durable subagent id, and keeps the child conversation available for later turns. When that run settles, the runtime sends the parent a notice containing its outcome and any final assistant message; `send_message` steers the child's nearest step while it is running and starts a turn while it is idle. Set `run_in_background: false` only when your next action depends on receiving the result.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the delegated task, for display.

prompt.description: The complete, self-contained task for the subagent. It does not share this conversation's context, so include everything it needs.

run_in_background.description: Whether to run in the background and return a durable subagent id immediately. Defaults to true. Set false to wait for the result when your next action depends on it.

tools.name: subagent_fork
tools.description: Delegate a task to a subagent that inherits this conversation: a child agent seeded with all completed turns so far (it does not see the current in-flight turn). Use this when the subtask builds on this conversation's context — a follow-up analysis, a review, a continuation — without consuming this conversation's context for the work itself. You receive its result, not its intermediate steps. This tool runs in the background by default, immediately returns a durable subagent id, and keeps the child conversation available for later turns. When that run settles, the runtime sends the parent a notice containing its outcome and any final assistant message; `send_message` steers the child's nearest step while it is running and starts a turn while it is idle. Set `run_in_background: false` only when your next action depends on receiving the result.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the delegated task, for display.

prompt.description: The task for the subagent. It already sees this conversation's completed turns, so build on them freely and state only what is new.

run_in_background.description: Whether to run in the background and return a durable subagent id immediately. Defaults to true. Set false to wait for the result when your next action depends on it.

tools.name: todo_write
tools.description: Record and update a structured task list for the current work. Send the ENTIRE list every call — it REPLACES the previous list (there are no partial updates, no per-item edits). Use it to plan multi-step work and show progress: add one todo per concrete step before you start. Mark every todo being actively worked on `in_progress` — several at once when work genuinely runs in parallel (e.g. concurrent subagents or background commands), one for sequential work; while work remains, at least one task should be `in_progress`. Mark a todo `completed` the moment it is done (do not batch completions), and allow no `in_progress` item only once all work is complete. Skip the list for trivial single-step tasks. Statuses: `pending` (not started), `in_progress` (being worked on now), `completed` (finished).

todos.description: The COMPLETE task list, replacing any previous list.

content.description: What the task is — a short imperative line.

tools.name: update_goal
tools.description: Update the exact current goal revision. edit, pause, and resume require a direct top-level human request. During an automatic continuation of the current goal, complete and blocked are also allowed. blocked is rejected before the configured minimum round count; the model remains responsible for judging that the same condition persisted across those rounds and must explain it in blocked_reason.

revision.description: Exact positive revision returned by get_goal.

action.description: edit | pause | resume | complete | blocked

objective.description: Replacement objective; valid only with action edit.

max_goal_rounds.description: Replacement cap; valid only with action edit.

blocked_reason.description: Concrete blocking condition; required only with action blocked.

tools.name: web_fetch
tools.description: Fetch the content of a specific HTTP(S) URL and return it decoded to text.

tools.name: web_search
tools.description: Search the web for current information. Provide 1–4 queries in the required queries array. Returns an optional summary answer and a list of source URLs.

queries.description: Required search queries; accepts 1–4 items and merges their results.

tools.name: workflow
tools.description:
Run a JavaScript workflow script that orchestrates subagents at scale. Use this for work that fans out across many independent pieces — an audit over many files, a migration, multi-angle research, adversarial verification of findings — where you write the orchestration as a script instead of delegating turn by turn.

The workflow's identity rides the `meta` parameter as JSON: required `name` (short kebab-case) and `description` strings, optional `whenToUse` string and `phases` array (`{title, detail?, provider?, model?}`). The `script` parameter is the plain JavaScript body ONLY (NOT TypeScript, and NO `export const meta` statement — meta is a parameter, not code), running with top-level await; end with `return <value>` — the value must be JSON-serializable and is this tool's result.

Script-body hooks:
- `agent(prompt, opts?): Promise<any>` — run one subagent to completion. Without `opts.schema` it resolves to the child's final text; with `opts.schema` (an object-rooted JSON Schema using ONLY type/properties/required/additionalProperties/items/enum/const/oneOf — no pattern/format/numeric bounds) it resolves to the validated object. Resolves `null` when the child fails (filter with `.filter(Boolean)`). Other opts: `label` (display), `phase` (progress group), and independent `provider`/`model` LLM target overrides (either may be provided alone). Anything else (`effort`/`isolation`/`agentType`) is rejected loudly.
- `pipeline(items, ...stages): Promise<any[]>` — run each item through the stages independently with NO barrier between stages (prefer this for multi-stage work). Each stage receives `(prev, item, index)`. An ordinary stage throw drops that ITEM to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- `parallel(thunks): Promise<any[]>` — run zero-argument functions concurrently and await ALL of them (a barrier; use only when a stage genuinely needs every prior result together). A throwing thunk resolves to `null`.
- `phase(title)` — start a progress phase; `log(message)` — narrate progress; `args` — the tool call's `args` input, verbatim.

Misused hooks (bad arguments, unknown options, unsupported schemas, tripped caps) throw errors that ALWAYS kill the script — they never dissolve into a per-item `null`.

Constraints: concurrency and total-agent caps apply; no filesystem, network, timers, or Node.js APIs are provided — the agents do the work, the script only coordinates them. The run executes in the foreground: this call returns when the whole script finishes.

script.description: The plain-JS workflow script body (top-level await allowed; NO `export const meta` statement; end with `return <json-value>`).

meta.description: The workflow identity block (plain JSON — never code).

name.description: Short kebab-case workflow name.

description.description: One-line description of what the workflow does.

whenToUse.description: Optional guidance on when this workflow applies.

phases.description: Optional phase declarations matched by phase() calls.

title.description: The phase title phase() calls match by exact string.

detail.description: Optional one-line description of the phase.

provider.description: Optional provider override this phase is expected to use.

model.description: Optional model override this phase is expected to use.

args.description: Optional JSON input exposed to the script as the `args` global (wrap a bare list as a field, e.g. {"files": [...]}).

file_path.description: Path to write, resolved by the filesystem backend.

content.description: Full UTF-8 text content to write.

justification.description: Required with sandbox_permissions: one sentence for the user explaining why this exact file operation needs the wider access.

Excellent — critical findings:

1. **`@deepseek-ai/dsh`: `latest` = 0.1.7-rc.2** (also `next` = 0.1.7-rc.2). So `npm i -g @deepseek-ai/dsh` (no version) gets 0.1.7-rc.2. ✓

   This matters because the profile's `dsh.profile.bundles` lists `@deepseek-ai/dsh-base` and `@deepseek-ai/dsh-web-app` — but those resolve from the dsh install dir's own node_modules (as dependencies of the `dsh` package, pinned to `^0.1.7-rc.2`), not by tag. So the upgrade via `npm i -g @deepseek-ai/dsh@0.1.7-rc.2` will pull `@deepseek-ai/dsh-base@0.1.7-rc.2` etc. as its dependencies. Good.
   
   Hmm, but wait: does `@deepseek-ai/dsh@0.1.7-rc.2` depend on `@deepseek-ai/dsh-base@^0.1.7-rc.2`? Then npm resolves `^0.1.7-rc.2` → the highest matching prerelease = 0.1.7-rc.2 (since 0.1.7-rc.2's tuple matches). Fine.

3. **`profiles\node_modules` has 244 @deepseek-ai packages at 0.1.5-rc.3** — how were they installed? No `profiles\package.json`, no lockfile. So something created `profiles\node_modules` without a manifest... That's odd. Possibly the dsh boot creates a "module fallback" by installing packages there? Or `profiles\web\.dsh-module-fallback\node_modules` is the fallback and `profiles\node_modules` came from an npm install run in that dir (npm can install without a package.json? `npm i <pkg>` creates one. Hmm, but there's no package.json — maybe it was deleted, or the install used `--no-save`).

   Whatever the origin, these are **stale 0.1.5-rc.3 duplicates**. After upgrading the CLI to 0.1.7-rc.2, if the profile resolution falls back to `profiles\node_modules`, we'd get a mixed 0.1.7 CLI + 0.1.5 libraries — a classic recipe for weird breakage.

   Per the docs: "dsh.profile.bundles 中列出的组合包先从 dsh 安装目录解析（@deepseek-ai/dsh-base、@deepseek-ai/dsh-web-app、…），再从 profile 自身的 node_modules 解析". So bundles resolve from the install dir FIRST → new versions. But other module resolution (e.g., plugins importing `@deepseek-ai/dsh-client-runtime`) might resolve via Node's normal algorithm from the profile dir → `profiles\web\node_modules` (empty) → `profiles\node_modules` (0.1.5-rc.3!) → could load OLD client libraries alongside a NEW host. That's a real risk.

   This is getting deep. The pragmatic approach: after upgrading, check whether the stale `profiles\node_modules` (0.1.5-rc.3) is used at all. Safest: **also upgrade or remove the stale tree**. Options:
   - (a) Upgrade it: since there's no manifest, I could run `npm install --prefix C:\Users\徐丰哲\.dsh\profiles @deepseek-ai/dsh-base@0.1.7-rc.2 ...` — messy (244 packages).
   - (b) Rename it aside (`profiles\node_modules.old-<ts>`) so resolution falls through to the fresh install dir. But if the *host* relies on it for something, renaming breaks the boot. Since the docs say bundles resolve from the install dir first, and the profiles dir previously worked *with* this tree at the same version as the CLI... hmm, wait: `profiles\node_modules` contains 244 packages including `@deepseek-ai/dsh` itself (0.1.5-rc.3)! Interesting — so someone/something installed the whole dsh distribution there.

   Let me investigate where it's actually used: check `.dsh-module-fallback\node_modules` content (it's a dir) and look for symlinks? Earlier listing showed `profiles\web\.dsh-module-fallback\node_modules` as a directory. Let me check what's inside it (maybe symlinks/junctions to profiles\node_modules!).

   That would explain everything: `.dsh-module-fallback\node_modules` might be a junction → `profiles\node_modules`, created by the boot to give the profile a module fallback.

   Let me check: `Get-Item profiles\web\.dsh-module-fallback\node_modules | Select LinkType, Target`.

4. Global install: `dsh@0.1.5-rc.3` + `pnpm@12.6.0` in prefix `%APPDATA%\npm`; dsh dir = 213.9 MB; global node_modules = 663.5 MB.

5. Also: after upgrading the CLI, does the **profile's own `node_modules`** (currently empty) + the fallback matter? And `dshmarket` was installed into `profiles\web\node_modules` with pnpm (hoisted) → pnpm created `profiles\web\node_modules\.pnpm` + `dshmarket`. Its deps (js-yaml, argparse) are there. Fine.

Plan:
1. Investigate the `.dsh-module-fallback` structure to understand the stale tree's role.
2. Then decide: stage 0.1.7-rc.2 + verify + swap; and handle the stale `profiles\node_modules` (rename aside if it's a fallback target — but that could break the old host until restart; better: rename AFTER the swap, or upgrade it too).

Actually, cleanest: after the swap, run `dsh --profile web --dump-config` again (which boots the config pipeline) to see if it works with the new CLI. If the module fallback is used, we'd see errors. Then decide.

content.text:
Now I understand the architecture precisely:

- `~/.dsh/profiles/node_modules` is a **module fallback directory** whose entries are **symlinks/proxies** pointing into the **install anchor** (the dsh install dir's node_modules). `healProfilesModuleFallback` at boot:
  - computes `resolveModuleFallbackEntries(installAnchor)` → the dependency closure of the installed `@deepseek-ai/dsh` package,
  - if the fallback isn't current, rewrites the links (symlinks or "module proxies"),
  - `packageNames` = installation-owned names.
- `~/.dsh/profiles/web/.dsh-module-fallback/node_modules` (currently empty) is for **bundle-owned** packages (per-profile), and the profile's own `node_modules` gets symlinks to those (see healProfileModuleFallback: `profileModulesDir` + `ownedModulesDir`).

So the "244 packages at 0.1.5-rc.3" in `profiles\node_modules` are **symlinks/proxies pointing at the 0.1.5-rc.3 install** — not a duplicate copy. They will be **automatically healed** to point at the new 0.1.7-rc.2 install dir at the next boot. That's why there's no package.json there.

Let me verify that they're symlinks (my earlier `Get-Item profiles\node_modules` showed no LinkType because it's the parent dir; I should check a child, e.g. `profiles\node_modules\@deepseek-ai\dsh-base` → LinkType/Target).

Also `profiles\node_modules\@deepseek-ai\dsh` = 0.1.5-rc.3 — the manifest read through the symlink → resolves to the install dir's package.json version. Makes sense.

So the upgrade concern is resolved: **the fallback is derived and self-healing**. After upgrading the global CLI, the next boot will heal the links to the new install. 

Also important: `moduleFallbackCurrent(modulesDir, entries)` compares versions → the heal happens automatically because the version changed. 

One more consideration: the fallback uses **symlinks**. Creating symlinks on Windows requires either Developer Mode or admin privileges! Hmm — but it worked before (the fallback presumably was created at first boot). Under DSH the host may have created them with a "module proxy" (kind === 'proxy') instead — `ensureModuleProxy(link, packageName, version, targets)` — that's probably a JS file that re-exports from the target, used when symlinks aren't available. Interesting: so on Windows without dev mode, it writes proxy files.

Either way: self-healing.

Now, the upgrade plan is clear and lower-risk than I feared:
1. Stage 0.1.7-rc.2 in a staging prefix under `D:\program_runtime_environment\_downloads\dsh-0.1.7-rc.2-stage` (per policy: installers/staging in _downloads), verify the staged CLI runs: `node <stage>\node_modules\@deepseek-ai\dsh\lib\bin.js --version` → 0.1.7-rc.2.
2. Swap: `npm install -g @deepseek-ai/dsh@0.1.7-rc.2 --registry <mirror>` (cache warm from staging → fast).
3. Verify: `dsh --version` → 0.1.7-rc.2.
4. Then (safe, non-destructive) verify the profile composes under the new CLI: `dsh --profile web --dump-config` → but this writes `profiles\web\cordis.yml` and *heals the module fallback* (rewrites `profiles\node_modules` symlinks to the new install!). Hmm — is that safe while the old host is running? The old host (PID 14036, 0.1.5-rc.3) has its modules already loaded; changing the fallback symlinks to point at the NEW install could break the old host if it lazy-loads something through the fallback (e.g., client plugin bundles). Risk!

   So: running `--dump-config` after the swap could destabilize the running host. Hmm. But the user must restart anyway to get 0.1.7. The question is whether the old host survives until they restart. To be safe, maybe:
   - Do NOT run the new CLI's boot/dump (which heals the fallback) until the user restarts.
   - Verify only that the *installed* files are correct: `dsh --version` (that runs the CLI's bin, which... does it heal? `dsh --version` goes through commander and exits before prepareProfile — likely no healing. Good.)
   
   So: after the swap, verify `dsh --version` only; leave the fallback healing to the first real boot after the user restarts. And warn the user that the running GUI may be unstable until they restart (they were going to restart for dshmarket anyway).

   Hmm, actually: will the *old host* even notice? It's running from memory with modules loaded. Node caches ESM modules by resolved URL; the resolved paths for the old install still exist (the old install dir is replaced by npm — the path is the same! `%APPDATA%\npm\node_modules\@deepseek-ai\dsh`, just with new content). So even re-reads would get new files. Mostly fine. The risk is low; the user restarts soon.

5. Rollback: `npm install -g @deepseek-ai/dsh@0.1.5-rc.3 --registry <mirror>` (documented).

Additional consideration: **dshmarket compatibility with 0.1.7.** The market's README said it supports up to 0.1.7 (it mentioned "dsh 0.1.7 及更新版本上没有这个开关可关" and "设置卡片——dsh 0.1.0-rc.7 起"). So it should be OK. Also `dsh-plugin-marketplace` (the other one) requires ≥0.1.7 — after this upgrade, the user could install that too if they want. Worth mentioning.

Also: `pnpm 12.6.0` and the profiles/web workspace config — unaffected.

Another important check: does 0.1.7-rc.2 require a newer Node? Let me check its `engines` field. Node here is 24.20.0 (very new) — fine. Let me verify engines anyway in the staged install.

Also, the profile's `dsh.profile.patchReload: live` etc. — unchanged.

One more: the staged install and swap will download ~214 MB (the dsh dir) + its deps (global node_modules is 663 MB total, but much of that is pnpm + shared deps already present). At 3.1 MB/s from the mirror → several minutes. With npm's cache (D:\...\_caches\npm) partially warm from the failed attempt, still mostly cold. So the whole thing might take 5-15 minutes. I must run it in the **background** to avoid the 600s cap killing it mid-install (which happened before!). Background + poll is the right approach here.

Let me write the upgrade script:
- `-Version '0.1.7-rc.2'` default (explicit, since `latest` on dsh is 0.1.7-rc.2 but being explicit is safer)
- `-Registry 'https://registry.npmmirror.com'`
- Steps: record current → stage → verify staged → install -g → verify → report.
- Save the full log to `logs\<conv>\...-upgrade-dsh.log`? The script's stdout will be captured by the job output; I'll also write a log file.
- Backup: record `npm ls -g --depth=0` output + the old package.json copy into `_downloads\dsh-<ver>-backup-<ts>\`. Copying the 214 MB dir as a backup is heavy — instead, record the version + the shim paths, and document the exact rollback command. I could also `npm pack` the old version? No. Rollback via reinstall is fine (0.1.5-rc.3 is on the registry).

Let me write the script and run it in the background.

Note: `npm install -g` on Windows with a running process holding files — npm may fail with EBUSY/EPERM if a file is locked. Node on Windows keeps .node/.dll files loaded (e.g., `sharp`, `node-pty`, `koffi` native addons). Those ARE locked by the running host! `npm install -g` would try to delete the old tree → **EBUSY on locked native modules** → install fails partway, potentially leaving a broken install!

This is a serious risk: `@deepseek-ai/dsh`'s global install contains native modules (node-pty, sharp, koffi, node-addon-*). The running host (PID 14036) has loaded some of them (node-pty for the terminal, koffi, etc.) → **their DLLs are locked** → npm cannot delete/replace them → the upgrade will fail with EBUSY/EPERM.

So an in-place upgrade of a running DSH install is very likely to FAIL. That's why the correct procedure is: **stop the host → upgrade → start the host.**

And I cannot stop the host (it's my own process). Therefore the honest, correct answer: I prepare everything (stage + verify + write a one-command upgrade script), and the user runs the actual swap after stopping `dsh web`. Or I can run a script that: (1) does the staging now, (2) writes a "do the swap" script, and (3) the user runs it (or asks me to run it) after closing the host.

Hmm, but that leaves the user to do the restart+swap. Alternatively: I could do the swap and accept that it may fail with EBUSY; if it fails, the install might be left broken (npm usually rolls back, but not always). Too risky.

Best approach (and I should be upfront): 
1. Stage 0.1.7-rc.2 into the npm cache + a staging prefix now (this is the slow part: download ~200-400 MB) and verify the new CLI runs from staging. **No risk** to the running host.
2. Write `scripts\conv-.../upgrade-dsh.ps1` that performs the actual global swap (and verification + rollback instructions), which must run while the host is stopped.
3. Tell the user: close the `dsh web` terminal (or stop PID 14036), then run the script (I give the exact command), then start `dsh web` again. Or if they prefer, they can ask me to run it and I'll do it in the same session — but then my session dies mid-run (the harness dies with the host) → the swap would be interrupted! So no: the swap MUST be run outside the DSH host process. Even a detached script launched by me would die? No — if I launch a *detached* background process (e.g., via Start-Process with -WindowStyle Hidden or a scheduled task), it survives the host's death. Hmm! That's a clever option: I could launch a detached PowerShell that waits for the host to exit, then performs the upgrade, then restarts `dsh web`. But: (a) the guidance says don't start a replacement server unless asked; (b) auto-restarting their GUI is intrusive; (c) the user asked to "upgrade the harness", which implies they accept a restart.

I think the right move: 
- Do the safe part now (stage + verify = the bulk of the work).
- Prepare the swap script.
- Ask the user how they want the final step done: (a) they run the script after stopping the host (recommended, safest), or (b) I launch a detached helper that stops the host, upgrades, and restarts `dsh web` automatically (one action, but interrupts this session and auto-restarts the server).

That's a genuine choice with tradeoffs → ask_user_question is appropriate. But I should do the staging FIRST (it's needed either way), then ask. Staging takes minutes → run in background.

tools.name: pwsh
tools.description: Execute a PowerShell command (`pwsh -Command`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh pwsh process; pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Paths use native Windows form (`C:\...`); read environment variables with `$env:NAME`. Managed `$env:DSH_*` variables expose current harness environment facts. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. On Windows a force-killed command settles as `[exit code: 1]` without a signal marker — treat it as an interruption, not a command failure. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]`, a policy denial: do not retry another way. Under the Windows sandbox, read-only pwsh runs in PowerShell ConstrainedLanguage mode, while workspace-write stays in FullLanguage unless host policy says otherwise. In read-only, prefer cmdlets and core types (`[string]`, `[datetime]`, `[regex]`, `[guid]`); .NET static calls (`[System.IO.*]::`, `[math]::`), `Add-Type`, COM objects, and reflection fail with "only core types" errors. `-f` formatting, property access, and core cmdlets work. In both confined modes, programs cannot open named pipes, so a command that captures another program's output through piped stdio (Node.js `child_process.spawn`/`exec` with the default `stdio: 'pipe'`) fails with EPERM, while `stdio: 'inherit'` and `stdio: 'ignore'` spawns work and PowerShell's own pipelines are unaffected. That EPERM is the documented boundary: do not retry the command another way — escalate the exact command once or restructure it to avoid capturing output.

tools.description:
Run a JavaScript workflow script that orchestrates subagents at scale. Use this for work that fans out across many independent pieces — an audit over many files, a migration, multi-angle research, adversarial verification of findings — where you write the orchestration as a script instead of delegating turn by turn.

Script-body hooks:
- `agent(prompt, opts?): Promise<any>` — run one subagent to completion. Without `opts.schema` it resolves to the child's final text; with `opts.schema` (an object-rooted JSON Schema using ONLY type/properties/required/additionalProperties/items/enum/const/oneOf) it resolves to the validated object. Resolves `null` when the child fails (filter with `.filter(Boolean)`). Other opts: `label` (display), `phase` (progress group), and independent `provider`/`model` LLM target overrides.
- `pipeline(items, ...stages): Promise<any[]>` — run each item through the stages independently with NO barrier between stages (prefer this for multi-stage work). Each stage receives `(prev, item, index)`. A stage throw drops that ITEM to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- `parallel(thunks): Promise<any[]>` — run zero-argument functions concurrently and await ALL of them (a barrier; use only when a stage genuinely needs every prior result together). A throwing thunk resolves to `null`.
- `phase(title)` — start a progress phase; `log(message)` — narrate progress; `args` — the tool call's `args` input, verbatim.

Misused hooks (bad arguments, unknown options, unsupported schemas, tripped caps) end the whole script instead of producing `null`. The script has no filesystem, network, timer, or Node.js APIs; the agents do the work.

tools.name: pwsh
tools.description: Execute a PowerShell command (`pwsh -Command`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh pwsh process; pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Paths use native Windows form (`C:\...`); read environment variables with `$env:NAME`. Managed `$env:DSH_*` variables expose current harness environment facts. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. On Windows a force-killed command settles as `[exit code: 1]` without a signal marker — treat it as an interruption, not a command failure. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]`, a policy denial: do not retry another way. Under the Windows sandbox, read-only pwsh runs in PowerShell ConstrainedLanguage mode, while workspace-write stays in FullLanguage unless host policy says otherwise. In read-only, prefer cmdlets and core types (`[string]`, `[datetime]`, `[regex]`, `[guid]`); .NET static calls (`[System.IO.*]::`, `[math]::`), `Add-Type`, COM objects, and reflection fail with "only core types" errors. `-f` formatting, property access, and core cmdlets work. In both confined modes, programs cannot open named pipes, so a command that captures another program's output through piped stdio (Node.js `child_process.spawn`/`exec` with the default `stdio: 'pipe'`) fails with EPERM, while `stdio: 'inherit'` and `stdio: 'ignore'` spawns work and PowerShell's own pipelines are unaffected. That EPERM is the documented boundary: do not retry the command another way — escalate the exact command once or restructure it to avoid capturing output.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "Get-Process" → "List running processes".

timeoutMs.description: Timeout in milliseconds. The executor applies its configured default and cap; on expiry the command moves to the background as a job instead of being killed.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

tools.name: workflow
tools.description:
Run a JavaScript workflow script that orchestrates subagents at scale. Use this for work that fans out across many independent pieces — an audit over many files, a migration, multi-angle research, adversarial verification of findings — where you write the orchestration as a script instead of delegating turn by turn.

Script-body hooks:
- `agent(prompt, opts?): Promise<any>` — run one subagent to completion. Without `opts.schema` it resolves to the child's final text; with `opts.schema` (an object-rooted JSON Schema using ONLY type/properties/required/additionalProperties/items/enum/const/oneOf) it resolves to the validated object. Resolves `null` when the child fails (filter with `.filter(Boolean)`). Other opts: `label` (display), `phase` (progress group), and independent `provider`/`model` LLM target overrides.
- `pipeline(items, ...stages): Promise<any[]>` — run each item through the stages independently with NO barrier between stages (prefer this for multi-stage work). Each stage receives `(prev, item, index)`. A stage throw drops that ITEM to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- `parallel(thunks): Promise<any[]>` — run zero-argument functions concurrently and await ALL of them (a barrier; use only when a stage genuinely needs every prior result together). A throwing thunk resolves to `null`.
- `phase(title)` — start a progress phase; `log(message)` — narrate progress; `args` — the tool call's `args` input, verbatim.

Misused hooks (bad arguments, unknown options, unsupported schemas, tripped caps) end the whole script instead of producing `null`. The script has no filesystem, network, timer, or Node.js APIs; the agents do the work.

title.description: The phase title phase() calls match by exact string.

args.description: Optional JSON input exposed to the script as the `args` global (wrap a bare list as a field, e.g. {"files": [...]}).

run_in_background.description: Run as a background job: return a job id immediately instead of waiting; the return value arrives with the completion notice.

The user asks: "我的电脑上有超级小爱建有本地知识库你如何可以调用" — "My computer has Super Xiao Ai (超级小爱) which has built a local knowledge base; how can you call/invoke it?"

"超级小爱" (Super Xiao Ai) is Xiaomi's AI assistant (小爱同学 — Xiao Ai). "超级小爱" is the newer version (HyperOS's Super Xiao Ai, 2024+). The user says it has built a local knowledge base (本地知识库) on their computer.

So the question: how can I (DSH agent) access/call it?

I need to investigate what's actually on this machine:
1. Is there a Xiaomi app installed (e.g., 小米妙享 / 超级小爱 / MiAI / 小米电脑助手 / HyperOS Connect / 小米云盘 — I saw `小米云盘` on D: earlier!)? 
2. Is there a local service/API (port), a database file, or a local knowledge base store (SQLite/vector DB)?
3. Does anything expose an API (HTTP/local port, MCP server, CLI)?

Known facts about 超级小爱 (Super Xiao Ai) on Windows: Xiaomi released "超级小爱" for PC as part of 小米澎湃OS / 小米电脑管家? Actually 超级小爱 PC 版 exists (小爱同学 PC 版 / 超级小爱 for Windows). It may store data locally. A "本地知识库" feature — 超级小爱 has a "本地知识库" / "个人知识库" feature? Hmm. In 2025 Xiaomi's 超级小爱 added "小爱记忆" and possibly local RAG over documents.

Since this is a real machine (the user's), I should investigate empirically rather than speculate:
- Search installed programs / program files / AppData for Xiaomi/XiaoAi related dirs and services.
- Check listening ports and running processes for anything Xiaomi-related.
- Look for local data stores (SQLite/Chroma/LanceDB/FAISS index files).
- Check for any local HTTP API.

Then answer: what's possible — e.g., if there's a local HTTP API, I could call it via PowerShell (with approval for network? localhost HTTP should be fine). If it's only a proprietary store, I could read the files if unencrypted (SQLite) — but that's fragile/unsupported. If there's no API, the honest answer: I can't "call" it directly; the practical integrations are (a) export documents into the workspace for me to read, (b) if it exposes an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, I could use it.

Also relevant: DSH has MCP client support (`dsh-mcp-client`) — if the knowledge base offers an MCP server, I could wire it. And DSH has skills. So a legitimate pathway would be: find an API/MCP/CLI, then integrate.

Let me investigate the machine thoroughly:
1. `Get-Process` for Xiaomi-ish names (小爱, XiaoAi, MiAI, Xiaomi, MiConnect, MiShare...).
2. Check `%LOCALAPPDATA%`, `%APPDATA%`, `C:\Program Files`, `C:\Program Files (x86)`, `D:\Application` (I saw `D:\Application\lceda-pro` in machine PATH, and `D:\Application` exists) for Xiaomi dirs.
3. Check listening ports: netstat -ano and map to processes (Get-NetTCPConnection was denied, but netstat worked).
4. Search for knowledge-base-ish files (sqlite, .db, vector indexes) under Xiaomi dirs.
5. Check installed software registry (Uninstall keys) for Xiaomi/小爱 entries.
6. Check services (Get-Service | Where DisplayName matches 小米/Xiaomi/Mi).

Note the sandbox limits: reading outside the workspace is allowed (reads are generally permitted). Let me be careful with the huge searches (e.g., scanning all of C:) — target likely locations.

Let me start the recon. I'll do a few parallel commands:
- Command A: processes + services + listening ports (filtered).

2. **UI automation** — I could drive its window via UI Automation (WPF/WebView2), but that's fragile.
3. **Read its SQLite directly** — if the KB is in a plain SQLite file, I could query it read-only. But it may be encrypted or use a proprietary vector format; also 超级小爱 might lock it.
4. **Ask 超级小爱 for an export** — the user could export the KB; not an API.

(a) Find the KB's source-file list / storage and, if readable, query it (best case: SQLite with FTS).
(b) If it's a local service with an API, script it.
(c) Otherwise: the KB content can be exported or the sources identified, and I can read them directly — a documented, reliable path.

content.arguments:
{"command": "$xa = 'C:\Program Files\MI\XiaoaiAgent\3.0.4.289'
Write-Output '=== Channel.ini ==='
Get-Content -LiteralPath (Join-Path $xa 'Channel.ini') -Raw
Write-Output '=== apps_ctrl_open.json (first 1200 chars) ==='
$t = Get-Content -LiteralPath (Join-Path $xa 'apps_ctrl_open.json') -Raw
Write-Output $t.Substring(0, [Math]::Min(1200, $t.Length))
Write-Output ''
Write-Output '=== dist\provider (possible API endpoint configs) ==='
Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath (Join-Path $xa 'dist\provider') -Recurse -Force -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object -First 20 @{n='rel';e={$_.FullName.Substring($xa.Length)}}, Length | Format-Table -AutoSize | Out-String -Width 140
Write-Output '=== locally opened ports hint: any http server strings in the app configs? ==='
Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath $xa -Recurse -Force -File -Include '*.json' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
  Where-Object { $_.Length -lt 200000 -and $_.FullName -notmatch 'WebView' } |
  ForEach-Object {
    $c = [System.IO.File]::ReadAllText($_.FullName, [System.Text.Encoding]::UTF8)
    if ($c -match '127\.0\.0\.1:\d{4,5}|localhost:\d{4,5}') {
      $m = [regex]::Matches($c, '(127\.0\.0\.1|localhost):\d{4,5}') | Select-Object -First 3 -ExpandProperty Value
      Write-Output ('  ' + $_.FullName.Substring($xa.Length) + ' -> ' + ($m -join ', '))
    }
  }
Write-Output '=== large, recently modified files under MI dirs (last 45 days, >100 KB) ==='
$cut = (Get-Date).AddDays(-45)
foreach ($r in @('C:\ProgramData\MI', (Join-Path $env:LOCALAPPDATA 'MI'))) {
  Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath $r -Recurse -Force -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Where-Object { $_.Length -gt 100KB -and $_.LastWriteTime -gt $cut -and $_.FullName -notmatch 'AIModel|EBWebView|AICreator' } |
    Sort-Object LastWriteTime -Descending | Select-Object -First 15 |
    ForEach-Object { Write-Output ('  ' + $_.LastWriteTime.ToString('yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm') + '  ' + [Math]::Round($_.Length/1MB,1) + ' MB  ' + $_.FullName) }
}", "description": "Look for API endpoints and KB data files", "timeoutMs": 300000}

{"command": "$py = @'
# inspect-mi-rag-manifest.py - reveal the structure and text content of a Xiaoai RAG manifest
import json, sys, os

def walk(node, path, out, depth=0):
    if depth > 4:
        return
    if isinstance(node, dict):
        for k, v in node.items():
            walk(v, path + [str(k)], out, depth + 1)
    elif isinstance(node, list):
        out.append((path, 'list', len(node), None))
        if node:
            walk(node[0], path + ['[0]'], out, depth + 1)
    else:
        out.append((path, type(node).__name__, len(str(node)), str(node)[:160]))

def main():
    path = sys.argv[1]
    with open(path, 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
        data = json.load(f)
    print('file  :', path)
    print('bytes :', os.path.getsize(path))
    print('top   :', type(data).__name__)
    if isinstance(data, dict):
        print('keys  :', list(data.keys())[:40])
    rows = []
    walk(data, [], rows)
    print('nodes :', len(rows))
    print('---- structure (first 45 nodes) ----')

tools.name: pwsh
tools.description: Execute a PowerShell command (`pwsh -Command`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh pwsh process; pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Paths use native Windows form (`C:\...`); read environment variables with `$env:NAME`. Managed `$env:DSH_*` variables expose current harness environment facts. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. On Windows a force-killed command settles as `[exit code: 1]` without a signal marker — treat it as an interruption, not a command failure. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]`, a policy denial: do not retry another way. Under the Windows sandbox, read-only pwsh runs in PowerShell ConstrainedLanguage mode, while workspace-write stays in FullLanguage unless host policy says otherwise. In read-only, prefer cmdlets and core types (`[string]`, `[datetime]`, `[regex]`, `[guid]`); .NET static calls (`[System.IO.*]::`, `[math]::`), `Add-Type`, COM objects, and reflection fail with "only core types" errors. `-f` formatting, property access, and core cmdlets work. In both confined modes, programs cannot open named pipes, so a command that captures another program's output through piped stdio (Node.js `child_process.spawn`/`exec` with the default `stdio: 'pipe'`) fails with EPERM, while `stdio: 'inherit'` and `stdio: 'ignore'` spawns work and PowerShell's own pipelines are unaffected. That EPERM is the documented boundary: do not retry the command another way — escalate the exact command once or restructure it to avoid capturing output.

tools.name: workflow
tools.description:
Run a JavaScript workflow script that orchestrates subagents at scale. Use this for work that fans out across many independent pieces — an audit over many files, a migration, multi-angle research, adversarial verification of findings — where you write the orchestration as a script instead of delegating turn by turn.

Script-body hooks:
- `agent(prompt, opts?): Promise<any>` — run one subagent to completion. Without `opts.schema` it resolves to the child's final text; with `opts.schema` (an object-rooted JSON Schema using ONLY type/properties/required/additionalProperties/items/enum/const/oneOf) it resolves to the validated object. Resolves `null` when the child fails (filter with `.filter(Boolean)`). Other opts: `label` (display), `phase` (progress group), and independent `provider`/`model` LLM target overrides.
- `pipeline(items, ...stages): Promise<any[]>` — run each item through the stages independently with NO barrier between stages (prefer this for multi-stage work). Each stage receives `(prev, item, index)`. A stage throw drops that ITEM to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- `parallel(thunks): Promise<any[]>` — run zero-argument functions concurrently and await ALL of them (a barrier; use only when a stage genuinely needs every prior result together). A throwing thunk resolves to `null`.
- `phase(title)` — start a progress phase; `log(message)` — narrate progress; `args` — the tool call's `args` input, verbatim.

Misused hooks (bad arguments, unknown options, unsupported schemas, tripped caps) end the whole script instead of producing `null`. The script has no filesystem, network, timer, or Node.js APIs; the agents do the work.

# Wireless Display Fix I guess

If you get signature error 0x800b0100 mean you have a different Windows build version, you will have to find the ESD package matching your build version on UUP dump or somewhere else.

**Windows update will not work if you have any "illegally" installed packages, you have to remove then via dism, update your Windows, then add them again to use Wireless Display.**
Which you might not need to repeat many times since Win 10 is in EOL and LTSCs aren't receiving any updates really.

A Lazy one click(kinda-sorta-ish) solution for the infamous:

```
Error: 87

A Windows capability name was not recognized.
 ```

problem you get when trying to add the "Wireless Display" feature on Windows 10 LTSC.

This happens because:
`Microsoft-Windows-WirelessDisplay-FOD-Package` requires `Microsoft-Windows-RegulatedPackages-Package`, which is excluded from LTSC.
According to abbodi1406.

This repo contains the necessary packages and a powershell script to fix just that.

I really should not be shipping UUP files so I highly recommend you getting them yourself from UUP dump or somewhere else:

https://uupdump.net/getfile.php?id=e2d7464a-c8cc-4779-ad1d-36699425f3d3&file=Microsoft-Windows-RegulatedPackages-Package.ESD

https://uupdump.net/getfile.php?id=e2d7464a-c8cc-4779-ad1d-36699425f3d3&file=Microsoft-Windows-RegulatedPackages-WOW64-Package.ESD

https://uupdump.net/getfile.php?id=e2d7464a-c8cc-4779-ad1d-36699425f3d3&file=Microsoft-Windows-Client-LanguagePack-Package_en-us-amd64-en-us.esd

After downloading them you should extract each of them to a different folder with 7-zip.
Then add them to your system with:
```
dism /Online /Add-Package /PackagePath:1\Microsoft-Windows-RegulatedPackages-Package~31bf3856ad364e35~amd64~~10.0.19041.1.mum

dism /Online /Add-Package /PackagePath:2\Microsoft-Windows-RegulatedPackages-wow64-package~31bf3856ad364e35~amd64~~10.0.19041.1.mum

dism /Online /Add-Package /PackagePath:3\update.mum
```

Or you can use this repo.
# Instructions

1. Download the whole repo
2. Unzip the thing
3. Run the powershell script as Administrator
4. Reboot
5. Run `DISM /Online /Add-Capability /CapabilityName:App.WirelessDisplay.Connect~~~~0.0.1.0` as Administrator, or just simply add the feature from Windows setting.

Microsoft PowerToys

Microsoft PowerToys is a collection of utilities that help you customize Windows and streamline everyday tasks.

Installation · Documentation · Blog · Release notes

Ruler](https://aka.ms/PowerToysOverview_ScreenRuler) | [ Shortcut Guide](https://aka.ms/PowerToysOverview_ShortcutGuide) | | [ Text Extractor](https://aka.ms/PowerToysOverview_TextExtractor) | [ Window Hopper](https://aka.ms/PowerToysOverview_WindowHopper) | [ Workspaces](https://aka.ms/PowerToysOverview_Workspaces) | | [ ZoomIt](https://aka.ms/PowerToysOverview_ZoomIt) | | | ## 📦 Installation For detailed installation instructions and system requirements, visit the [installation docs](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/powertoys/install). But to get started quickly, choose one of the installation methods below:

Download the .exe file from GitHub
Go to the [PowerToys GitHub releases](https://aka.ms/installPowerToys), scroll down and select **Assets** to reveal the installation files, and choose the one that matches your architecture and install scope. For most devices, that would be _x64 per-user_.
Microsoft Store
You can easily install PowerToys from the Microsoft Store:

WinGet
Download PowerToys from [WinGet](https://github.com/microsoft/winget-cli#installing-the-client). Updating PowerToys via winget will respect the current PowerToys installation scope. To install PowerToys, run the following command from the command line / PowerShell: - User scope installer (default) ```powershell winget install Microsoft.PowerToys -s winget ``` - Machine-wide scope installer ```powershell winget install --scope machine Microsoft.PowerToys -s winget ```
Other methods
There are [community driven install methods](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/powertoys/install#community-driven-install-tools) such as Chocolatey and Scoop. If these are your preferred install solutions, you can find the install instructions there.

Most contributions require you to agree to a [Contributor License Agreement (CLA)][oss-CLA] declaring that you grant us the rights to use your contribution and that you have permission to do so. Findings so far:
- PowerToys README doesn't list system requirements; it links to docs (which my fetcher can't reach reliably). I still need the min Windows version. Hmm.
- Search results confirm: **"Miracast isn't available since updating to 24H2"** ([Microsoft Q&A](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/3927345/miracast-isnt-available-since-updating-to-24h2-on)) → confirms Microsoft removed/deprecated the Miracast *receiver* ("无线显示器" optional feature) in Windows 11 24H2+. The user's Redmi is **25H2** → **it cannot be a Miracast receiver**. So screen-extension via Miracast is dead on the Win11 side.
- The other side (LTSC 2019 receiving) needs the risky RegulatedPackages hack (which I documented from the README) and build-matched packages (17763 from UUP dump) → hacky, may break Windows Update. Not recommended.
- Anker article: "How to Use a Second Laptop as a Monitor" — generic.
- CSDN question about capture-card-as-second-screen latency — relevant to my capture-card recommendation.

So for **屏幕扩展**, the realistic options are:
1. **spacedesk** (virtual display driver + viewer over LAN): needs verification of system requirements. Their manual page won't fetch. Let me try once more with a different URL (e.g., `https://manual.spacedesk.net/SystemRequirements.html` failed twice — maybe the site blocks the fetcher; try `https://www.spacedesk.net/` or Google cache). Or use search snippets. My knowledge: spacedesk supports Windows 10/11 (x64) as primary (driver) and the secondary device can be Windows/Android/iOS/HTML5 viewer. There's an important nuance: the Windows viewer requires... spacedesk's "spacedesk for Windows" viewer is a free download. And the driver requires Windows 10 1607+ I believe. LTSC 2019 (1809) should satisfy that.
   Risk: spacedesk driver on Win11 25H2 — they update regularly; should be OK. Also spacedesk is free for personal use, and it's a *virtual display*, not remote control — fits the constraint. Some people consider it "remote desktop"-ish, but it's really a virtual monitor over LAN.
   Note: spacedesk on the *secondary* (viewer) side shows the extended desktop in a window/fullscreen — it does transmit screen content over LAN, which is technically "screen streaming", but not remote *control*. It fits "屏幕扩展" intent. I should be explicit that it does stream pixels over LAN (so it's not "no software sharing at all") — but it's not a remote-control tool.
2. **USB HDMI 采集卡 + 副屏软件**: HDMI out from PC A → USB capture on PC B → full-screen preview (OBS/相机/PotPlayer). Latency: 60–150 ms typical; 1080p60 dongles ~¥100-200. This is the most "no-software-stack" approach (Windows 相机 app works). Caveat: the capture device must be UVC (driver-free). Also, HDMI out from the source laptop: both laptops have HDMI out (Xiaoxin Air 13 Pro has HDMI? Many thin laptops have only USB-C; need to check the user's ports—can't). Also HDCP content won't capture.
3. **便携显示器 (portable monitor)**: buy a USB-C/HDMI portable screen (~¥400-800) — the most reliable "extension" but it's not "using the other computer as a screen". Worth mentioning as the no-compromise option.
4. **Miracast**: mostly dead (Win11 24H2+ removed receiver; LTSC needs hacks). Mention as "不推荐/基本不可行" with the evidence.

For **一套键鼠控两机**:
1. **Microsoft PowerToys → Mouse Without Borders** (free, Windows-only, up to 4 PCs, clipboard + file drag-and-drop, hotkey to lock/switch). Need min OS: PowerToys requires Windows 10 1809? Let me settle this. I recall the docs saying: "PowerToys requires Windows 11 or Windows 10 version 1809 (build 17763) or later" — hmm, but I also recall more recent versions requiring 2004+. Since I can't fetch the docs page, let me check the PowerToys installer metadata? Not available locally.
   Let me try fetching the docs page through a不同 route: maybe `https://learn.microsoft.com/zh-cn/windows/powertoys/install` works (the earlier failure might be transient). Or use jsDelivr on the docs repo? The PowerToys docs are in `MicrosoftDocs/windows-dev-docs` (archived) → now `MicrosoftDocs/windows-dev-docs`? Hmm, the PowerToys docs source is in the PowerToys repo? There's a `doc/` folder in the repo but the public docs live in learn.microsoft.com (source in `MicrosoftDocs/windows-dev-docs` or a private repo).
   Alternative: check the release notes in the repo for "minimum Windows version" mentions: `https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/microsoft/PowerToys@main/doc/devdocs/...`. Hmm.
   Simplest: **search for the exact phrase** "PowerToys requires Windows 10 version" and read the snippet.
   
2. **Deskflow** (open-source Synergy successor): Windows 10/11 x64; supports Win10 1809+. Its winget page exists. Let me check the wings/requirements via a fetch of the Deskflow docs (deepwiki link appeared). Deskflow is a solid choice for LTSC 2019.
3. **Input Director**: Windows-only, free for personal, ancient (2016) but works on Win10; supports 1809 fine.
4. **ShareMouse**: freemium.
5. **USB 切换器 / KVM**: hardware, zero software, most reliable — a 2-port USB switch (¥30-80) or a KVM with HDMI (¥100-300). This is the "no software at all" answer.
6. **多模键鼠（蓝牙+2.4G，可切 2–3 台）**: ~¥100-300; the cleanest no-software approach if they're willing to buy a keyboard/mouse.
7. **Logitech Flow**: needs MX-series hardware.
8. **KDE Connect (Windows)**: for clipboard/file/notification, not cursor.
9. **Barrier**: older fork, likely superseded by Deskflow.

For **文件/剪贴板互通**:
- SMB shared folders / mapped drives (both machines on LAN)
- 就近共享 (Nearby Sharing, Win10 1803+)
- LocalSend (open source, cross-platform, no cloud)
- Syncthing (continuous sync)
- Clipboard: Deskflow/MWB handle it; or Windows built-in `Clipboard sync`? (Win10/11 clipboard history sync is via Microsoft account — both machines would need the same MS account; LTSC 2019 supports clipboard sync? The cloud clipboard feature requires... it's available in Win10 1809+; with a Microsoft account. That's another option.)
- KDE Connect for clipboard.

Also **audio**: not asked.

Also **直接连线的网络**: for stability, a direct Ethernet cable (if both have RJ45) or USB-C dock; or a cheap switch; or Wi-Fi (both on the same router). Also **USB4/Thunderbolt networking** — need to check if the models support it; can't verify. Mention briefly.

Now: this machine is the Redmi (Win11 25H2). I can verify locally: does it have Bluetooth? Wi-Fi? USB4? HDMI out? Let me check via PnP/net adapters — earlier `Get-NetAdapter` returned nothing (the output was empty; the command's output didn't appear — because the whole block printed nothing? The earlier recon printed ProductName etc. but Get-PnpDevice/Get-NetAdapter printed nothing → likely blocked by sandbox).

Let me try again with different cmdlets (Get-NetAdapter might need elevation; `Get-CimInstance Win32_NetworkAdapter` may be blocked too). Could use `systeminfo`? Blocked probably. Let me try `Get-PnpDevice -Class Net` etc. If all blocked, skip: I can ask the user about ports, or just present options generically with "看你的接口" notes.

Given time, the most useful deliverable: a **comparison document** (per my standard, in deliverables) + a concise inline summary. The user asked "给我看看有几种方案" → a survey. A document with a comparison table is genuinely useful for them to keep/share.

(a) PowerToys min Windows version (decides MWB on LTSC 1809).
(b) spacedesk Windows support/requirements.

Then write the doc.

For (a): try fetching `https://learn.microsoft.com/zh-cn/windows/powertoys/install` (retry).
For (b): try `https://www.spacedesk.net/` or the manual with http://.

Let me also check the LTSC machine's Miracast sending capability (it's fine, 1809 supports it) — no need.

Let me batch: 2 fetches + 1 search (for the exact PowerToys requirement phrase).

Actually — hmm, one important consideration about PowerToys on LTSC 2019: even if PowerToys supports 1809, its installer may require .NET 8/9 Desktop Runtime (fine) and the newer PowerToys versions target Win10 2004+? Let me just search for the phrase.

Let me run: 
1. web_fetch https://learn.microsoft.com/zh-cn/windows/powertoys/install
2. web_fetch https://www.spacedesk.net/
3. web_search ["PowerToys system requirements \"Windows 10\" version 1809 19041 install", "spacedesk 免费 虚拟显示器 Windows 客户端 下载 支持 Win10"]

Hmm. There's also the fact that current PowerToys (0.9x) requires **.NET 9 Desktop Runtime** and Windows 10 1809+... Microsoft's docs state: "PowerToys requires Windows 10 version 1809 (build 17763) or later" — I'm ~70% confident. But there were reports that newer PowerToys requires 2004+.

Since I can't verify, the honest approach: mark it as "需实测确认" and give the definitive alternatives. Also note that even if PowerToys installs, MWB works over LAN.

# 两台电脑互通方案（屏幕扩展 + 一套键鼠控两机）

## 0. 设备与已核实事实
| 机器 | 系统 | 备注 |
|---|---|---|
| 红米 Redmi 16 Pro 2026 | **Windows 11 家庭中文版 25H2（build 26200.9457）** — 本机实测（注册表 ProductName 仍写 "Windows 10 Home China" 是 Win11 的已知遗留字段） | 无 Miracast 接收能力（24H2 起微软已弃用"无线显示器"可选功能） |
| 联想 小新 Air 13 Pro 2026 | **Windows 10 LTSC 2019（build 17763，1809）** | 无应用商店；系统组件受限（下面会用到） |

已核实：
- PowerToys 0.101.2362.0 的 `MinimumOSVersion = 10.0.17134.0`（1803）→ **LTSC 2019 可用**
- 无商店的 LTSC 用不了 winget/Store 版 → 只能下 GitHub releases 的 .exe（我可以在这台下好给你）
- Miracast 接收：Win11 24H2 起被移除（微软 Q&A 有多例）；LTSC 2019 要当接收端必须用 UUP 补丁包强行装 `RegulatedPackages`，README 自己都警告会破坏 Windows Update → 不建议

## 1. 方案总览（按"是否远程控制"分类）
说明：你排斥的是"远程控制"（把对方的桌面接管、注入输入）。下面软件类方案里，**键鼠共享只传输入事件、虚拟显示器只传画面**，都不是远程控制。

### A. 一套键鼠控两机
A1. **PowerToys 无边框鼠标（Mouse Without Borders）** — 免费、微软官方、最多 4 台、剪贴板共享、支持在两机之间拖拽传文件、可用热键临时锁在单机。**两机都支持**（见上方核实）。走局域网，延迟低。
A2. **Deskflow**（Synergy/Barrier 的开源后继）— 跨平台、剪贴板共享、可配置布局；LTSC 亦可用。
A3. **Input Director** — Windows 专用，免费（个人），支持多显示器与热键，老牌稳定。
A4. **硬件 USB 切换器**（2 进 1 出，一键/热键切换）— ¥30–100，零软件零配置，最稳；缺点是不能"跨屏移动"，只能整体切换。
A5. **KVM 切换器（带 HDMI）** — ¥100–300，键鼠+显示器一起切换；适合"一台显示器轮流用两台主机"。
A6. **多模键鼠（蓝牙+2.4G，可切 2–3 台）** — ¥100–300；键盘按一下换机，鼠标按底下按钮换机；零软件。
A7. **Logitech Flow**（需 MX 系列键鼠）— 跨机移动+剪贴板+文件；硬件成本较高。
A8. **KDE Connect（Windows 版）** — 不做光标共享，但能互通剪贴板/文件/通知，可作为补充。

### B. 屏幕扩展（把另一台当第二屏）

# 无线投屏 / 屏幕扩展方案（红米 Win11 25H2 × 联想 Win10 LTSC 2019）

- 约束：**不用远程控制软件**（不接管对方桌面）；两台机器都在同一局域网

- 原理：宿主机跑 Deskreen 服务，**任何带浏览器的设备**打开链接就成为"第二屏"，走 Wi-Fi/局域网。

## 3. 推荐顺序（按你的约束）

| 你的偏好 | 选它 |
|---|---|
| 免费 + 开源 + 不想在联想那台装东西 | **Deskreen**（宿主红米，联想用浏览器） |
| 免费 + 要最像真第二屏 | **spacedesk**（我先实测再定） |
| 要低延迟/高画质，且不排斥"串流"性质 | **Sunshine + Moonlight** |
| 只想把联想画面镜像到红米看，接受付费 | **AirServer**（红米当接收端，联想用 Win+P 投） |
| 想要完全零软件 | ❌ 无线这条路做不到（只能上采集卡，但那是有线） |

## 4. 实测与落地（我可以做的）

1. **在红米这台（本机）先装并实测**：Deskreen（或 spacedesk），确认能创建虚拟显示器、能出画面。
2. 给联想那台输出**零安装的 browser 访问地址**（Deskreen 路线），你把地址在那台浏览器里打开即可。
3. 若选 spacedesk/Sunshine：我给出联想端的下载与配置步骤（你执行），你把 `ipconfig` 和报错贴回来，我据此调整。
4. 需要时我可以加好防火墙规则、固定端口、并写一个一键启动脚本放进 `scripts\`。

## 5. 已知限制（先说清楚，避免落差）

- 无线扩展屏**不适合看视频/玩游戏**（浏览器类延迟 100–300 ms）；看文档、放参考、监控窗口、写代码够用。
- 两台机器**必须在同一局域网**，且路由器不能开"AP 隔离"。
- 延迟随 Wi-Fi 质量波动；想稳定，可以两台各插一条网线到同一路由/交换机。
- 虚拟显示驱动属于显示适配器驱动，部分安全软件会提示（属正常）。

  This project creates a _virtual monitor_ in Windows that functions just like a physical display. It is particularly useful for applications such as **streaming, virtual reality, screen recording,** and **headless servers

  - **EDID integration**: Added EDID integration support for custom/virtual monitor profiles.
  This repository uses a Git submodule for Microsoft Windows Driver Frameworks headers. Clone with submodules enabled:
  - [Driver Installer (Windows 10/11)](https://github.com/VirtualDrivers/Virtual-Display-Driver/releases) - Check the [Releases](https://github.com/VirtualDrivers/Virtual-Display-Driver/releases) page for the latest versio
  - **Winget:** `winget install --id=VirtualDrivers.Virtual-Display-Driver -e`
  > Before using the Virtual Display Driver, ensure the following dependencies are installed:
  >   If you encounter the error `vcruntime140.dll not found`, download and install the latest version from the [Microsoft Visual C++ Redistributable page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/windows/latest-supported-vc-
  > **Driver update safety:** If you're about to install **major GPU/chipset driver updates**, uninstall VDD first. If you get a black screen or display priority gets scrambled, boot into **Safe Mode** and uninstall VDD to
  ## 🛠️ Installation
  - You can download the installer directly from the [Releases](https://github.com/VirtualDrivers/Virtual-Display-Driver/releases) page.
  - Click the Install button.
  - Step 3: Verify the Installation (Optional)
  - Check if the Virtual Display Driver is correctly installed by running the following:
  - **Settings:** Check display settings under system settings and see if the virtual displays show.
  While VDC is a good and friendly way to work with VDD, you can also do a a lot manually. Like adding or removing resolutions or enable/disable

- **Option 1 (scripted)**: devcon install → then check whether a virtual display appears. If the settings XML location matters, copy `vdd_settings.xml` to the documented spot. Hmm. Since I can't see the screen, a scripted install with verification is better for me to confirm success. And if the display count/resolution needs tweaking, the user can open VDD Control afterwards.

Let me look for the settings file location: the VDD docs (README) may have a "Settings" section explaining that `vdd_settings.xml` must be placed in the driver folder. Let me grep the README for the exact wording around 'xml' and 'settings' — the earlier output got truncated before those lines. Let me grep with a tighter filter: 'xml' only.

Actually — smarter: the zip contains `vdd_settings.xml` in each driver dir AND `Dependencies/vdd_settings.xml`. The VDD Control app probably copies the settings next to the installed driver files. Historically, VDD required putting `vdd_settings.xml` in `C:\VirtualDisplayDriver\` or in the directory containing the installed driver (e.g., `C:\Windows\System32\DriverStore\...`? no). Hmm.

Let me just check the README's "Settings" section text around 'xml'/'settings' to get the authoritative path. One more quick read with filter 'xml'.

Alternatively: do the devcon install and then *test empirically*: check `Get-PnpDevice -Class Display` and whether a new display appears (e.g., via `Get-CimInstance Win32_DesktopMonitor` or `Get-PnpDevice`). If the driver loads and creates 1 display by default, that's enough — the default settings likely work (the bundled vdd_settings.xml probably defines 1-2 monitors at common resolutions).

Also note: after the driver device is created, Windows may need a moment; and the display might be "extended" automatically (Windows usually extends to a new display by default).

```
1) stage installers to D:\program_runtime_environment\_downloads\{deskreen,vdd}\
2) extract vdd zip → D:\program_runtime_environment\cli\vdd-control\25.7.23\
3) verify signatures: mttvdd.cat + MttVDD.dll (Authenticode) 
4) devcon install "<...>\SignedDrivers\x86\VDD\MttVDD.inf" Root\MttVDD
5) verify: devcon status Root\MttVDD ; Get-PnpDevice -Class Display | findstr /i "virtual MttVDD"
6) install Deskreen: "<...>\deskreen-ce-3.2.16-x64.exe" /S ; wait ; verify installed exe
7) report
```

Wait — before the driver install, I should verify the .cat signature. Let me include that in the script and abort if invalid.

For devcon: it needs admin. Our escalation runs with the user's token — is it elevated? **The DSH escalation (danger-full-access) removes the sandbox restrictions but does NOT elevate to admin.** Installing a driver requires Administrator privileges. If the user's account is an admin but the process runs unelevated (medium integrity), `devcon install` will fail with "Access is denied" or the driver install will be rejected.

Hmm! That's a real issue. Earlier, `[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable(...,'User')` worked (user-level), and writing to Program Files... did I write to Program Files? I wrote to D:\program_runtime_environment and C:\Users\...\.dsh (user-writable). Program Files wasn't tested. Actually — the node install (python) installed to D:\program_runtime_environment\python (writable). So I haven't proven admin.

Let me check whether the current process is elevated: `[Security.Principal.WindowsPrincipal]::new([Security.Principal.WindowsIdentity]::GetCurrent()).IsInRole([Security.Principal.WindowsBuiltInRole]::Administrator)` — that's a .NET call (CoreCLR type) — should work in PowerShell under the sandbox? The sandbox restricts .NET static calls in *ConstrainedLanguage* (read-only mode); we're in workspace-write → FullLanguage. So it should work... but the sandbox may still block the token query. Let me try.

If not elevated: the driver install will need a UAC prompt. Options:
- Run the devcon install via `Start-Process -Verb RunAs` → triggers a UAC prompt the user must approve (they're at the machine). That's acceptable and explicit: I'll tell them "会弹一次 UAC，请点'是'"。
- Or have them run VDD Control as admin themselves and click Install.

Given the user approved installing the driver, using `Start-Process -Verb RunAs` with a UAC prompt is the cleanest path — but our escalated pwsh is itself launched headlessly; a UAC prompt would appear on their desktop and they'd click Yes. That works if they're watching. I should warn them.

Hmm, but there's a subtlety: if the DSH escalation itself grants admin (some harnesses run the escalated command with a different mechanism), then no UAC needed. Let me just test elevation status first — cheap and decisive.

Let me also check whether the Deskreen installer needs admin (Electron NSIS per-user: no) — so Deskreen can install unelevated.

1. Check elevation status + whether Secure Boot is on (matters for driver signing enforcement).
2. Read the README settings section for vdd_settings.xml placement (filter 'xml').
Then write and run the install script (with UAC handling).
